newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK BANKERS SAY CBANK MUST HELP WITH LIQUIDITY.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK BANKERS SAY CBANK MUST HELP WITH LIQUIDITY.

text.p: A slowdown in foreign capital inflows to Slovakia have caused an acute shortage of funds in the banking sector, prompting some bankers to call for a loosening of the central bank's monetary policy.
According to central bank figures, with banks' minimum reserve demands are fulfilled at only 97.49 percent as of Friday, in the face of the annual tax payments.
And some analysts warned that if the situation continues, bank's may be forced to sell off assets to gain liquidity, though this has not happened yet.

"If the money market liquidity fluctuates, as it does extraordinarily so at present, banks first of all liquidate their liquid cushion (assets)," Sylvia Majlingova, Liquidity Department Director at CSOB Bank, told Reuters.
"Unless the central bank (NBS) loosens its monetary policy the market seems headed for no greater stabilisation," she added.
Added Jaroslav Hora, chief dealer at VUB: "Liquidity is not coming from abroad, which is slowing down the sector from filling its requirements."
He said that while the sector will most likely meet the minimum reserve demands, it is doing it mainly through securities repo tenders by the central bank which cannot satisfy everyone's needs.
NBS Open Market Operation Department Director Peter Andresic told Reuters on Friday that the market is suffering more from interest rate instability than from liquidity fluctuations.

"There is an uncertainty on the market that some banks may fail to meet the minimum reserve demands, which is understandable. So far we have been adding liquidity on a daily basis this week," Andresic said, declining to comment further.

The banking sector faced a major liquidity crunch in January, failing to meet the overall minimum reserve requirement after the NBS limited bank refinancing, opting to hold repo tenders to curb loan expansion.
The move came shortly after the cabinet approved a 1997 state budget deficit of 3.7 percent of GDP, up from a 0.4 percent surplus in 1996.
The liquidity cruch, which boosted the interbank money market rates to record highs of 26 percent in January, was soon relaxed by an inflow of estimated $130-380 million.
But more one month later the funds had more or less left as deposit rates dropped, leaving the market volatile with longer-term depo rates stabilising at 17-18 percent.
Some analysts said the rates were still low enough to attract foreign deposits, but others saw Slovakia's burgeoning current account deficit behind foreign investor reluctance.

"Money is expensive, but demand for it lasts," said Ivan Boledovic, head of Slovenska Sporitelna Investment Banking Division. He added credit line problems between Slovak banks have forced many to turn to repo dealing for liquidity.
Analysts said that despite a repo rate increase for such deals to above 17-18 percent on all terms, traded volumes have been steady.
